They have campaigned on platforms promising to liberate their national polity from the perils of globalization and the immense, tangled bureaucracy of Brussels. The past half-decade has seen these parties creep ever closer to victory. Reform UK, the British party founded by Nigel Farage and running on an anti-immigration platform, is sitting in a comfortable lead over both establishment rivals. Alternative for Germany , a party deemed so right-wing by its opponents that mainstream lawmakers refuse to work with it, is dominating voter intention surveys. National Rally, the ever-present right-wing party of France , is on a path to victory despite the highly publicized conviction of its leader for financial crimes. Recommended Stories UK naval drones had components that secretly transmitted data to China Board of Peace undeterred by Israel’s rejection of peace plan at this stage Strong 7.4 magnitude earthquake strikes Colombia and neighboring Ecuador Germany , France, and the United Kingdom are three of the most pivotal players on the continent, and all of these right-wing parties will have their chance to flip their nations in the next three years. From the outside looking in, Europe seems like a powder keg of nationalist, populist resentment preparing to explode across the continent. Advertisement A rally for supporters of France’s National Rally, and Alice Weidel speaks to supporters. (AP) The question is: If citizens across Europe do vote in a succession of right-wing parties to lead their most powerful governments, will these disparate groups be able to form a coherent movement? The Hungarian connection Hungary, formerly governed by Prime Minister Viktor Orban , successfully positioned itself as the Western world’s beacon of national conservatism. The premier spent the better part of his time in high office building out infrastructure that spoke to a traditional, Christian, and nationalist mindset. He provided lavish tax breaks for women who had multiple children, established a state secretary position dedicated to aiding persecuted Christians, suppressed the public promotion of LGBT lifestyles, and flipped the middle finger at the European Union every chance he had. Orban embraced Hungary’s role as a global hub of right-wing ideology, flying over intelligentsia from other European countries and America, giving them cushy jobs at conservative think tanks and universities. Advertisement Orban’s worldwide relevance hit a fever pitch during the second administration of President Donald Trump , whom the Hungarian statesman had stayed loyal to even after his defeat in the 2020 election. Though nationalists are concerned primarily with the integrity of their own nations, few view this as contradicting the pursuit of international alliances with like-minded partners in an equal partnership. Some, such as Balazs Orban, the former prime minister’s political director, view such alliances as essential for the survival of independent nation-states. “The European right and everybody who cares about Western civilization should say, ‘We should win all of them.’ All of them,” Balazs Orban told the Washington Examiner in an interview, when asked how many elections in Europe had to be won in order to change the tide. Advertisement Hungary has punched far above its weight in this struggle, using the stability of the 16-year Fidesz party rule to create right-wing infrastructure that stretched across national borders, even extending across the Atlantic. Balazs Orban helped spearhead this struggle, founding the Mathias Corvinus Collegium in 2020, a conservative think tank that quickly established connections throughout the Western world. That Hungarian think tank and others have partnered with other international organizations to further plant their roots. Balazs Orban sees elections in Europe more like battles in a war for the soul of Western civilization, saying right-wing parties need unity, but more than that, they need thoughtful leadership. The kind of grandiose language pitching the current political fight as an existential struggle for the West is a common strain among nearly all European right-wing parties. Advertisement “Patriotic movements in the West are united by shared values ​​that forge us into a common movement: the democratic nation-state rather than supranational decision-making bodies; national sovereignty rather than external control; the preservation of national identity and culture rather than multiculturalism and ‘woke’ leftism; and a Christian — not Muslim — character. Yet, on this shared foundation, we naturally also have distinct national interests,” Beatrix von Storch, the deputy parliamentary group leader of AfD, told the Washington Examiner . Though Viktor Orban was ousted from power by Peter Magyar’s Tisza Party in April, he retains his leadership of Fidesz and has given no sign that he is ready to give up. “The struggle for the soul of Western civilization did not end when we lost the election,” the former prime minister told the Washington Examiner . “American and Hungarian patriots stand on the same side in this fight.” Advertisement His ousting and Magyar’s extensive efforts to purge the government of his influence have jeopardized much of the right-wing infrastructure built up over the past decade. United Kingdom: The odd one out One of the defining features of the various right-wing parties of Europe is their positions on a dialectic between an inward and outward focus — on this spectrum, Hungary can easily be considered the most outward-focused, while Reform UK is the most inward-focused. In fact, the party chafes at the propensity of observers to lump it in with a continent-wide right-wing movement. A Reform UK party supporter wears rosettes outside the party office on Friday, June 21, 2024, in Clacton-on-Sea, England. (AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth) “The situations are very, very different” in each European country, Lois Perry, director of Heartland UK/Europe, told the Washington Examiner in an interview. She is close with the party and familiar with its internal dynamics but not directly affiliated with it. “Reform actually would not describe themselves necessarily as a right-wing party in the traditional sense,” she added. “… They would describe themselves as a common-sense party, a normal people’s party, which is why they’re attracting so many votes from the traditional left and the traditional right.” Reform UK falls firmly into the French National Rally’s camp in its strong focus on optics and electability. This has earned it the scorn of some further right parties on the continent, many of which Perry said would dismiss Reform as “lightweights.” Perry said Reform UK doesn’t have “any particularly strong ties” to other parties or right-wing figures within Europe, saying that the only real ties are from personal friendships and other relationships. The closest relationship is with National Rally, a relationship solidified through ideological affinity and a mutual focus on optics, not to mention geographical proximity and a shared history. Reform’s predecessor, the Brexit Party, made a splash in the European Parliament before Brexit, and memories of Farage and other British figures clashing with pro-EU politicians still brings back strong feelings of nostalgia among many still in the bloc. “As a Hungarian nationalist, I understand why the British nationalists voted to leave the EU,” Balazs Orban said. “But it’s a missed opportunity for them, and I miss them inside the European Union, because it would be much better to fight together with them against the liberal centralization of Brussels.” Perry said the sentiment is common among the right-wing parties of Europe and was recently showcased during a visit to the European Parliament. “‘We miss you guys! We miss Nigel Farage. He was a character,’” she recalled lawmakers saying with a laugh. “So in terms of having charismatic backup, then yeah, I get that.” Despite the distancing from the EU, Reform is well aware that its fortunes are still influenced significantly by the results of upcoming elections on the continent. “In terms of realpolitik … when Reform is in government, when Nigel Farage is the prime minister of the United Kingdom, it would be a lot easier to deal with a government which is not pro-mass immigration,” Perry said. The AfD-RN split and problems of unity While the right-wing parties across Europe are mostly united in grand civilizational questions and their top priorities, primarily immigration, maintaining an international alliance based on national interests is never seamless. Balasz Orban said Germany and France’s right-wing parties are the most important to see succeed — a natural answer given they’re the two biggest power players on the continent. Unfortunately for the right-wing international, National Rally and Alternative for Germany get along the least of the major right-wing parties in Europe. RN distinguishes itself with its focus on optics and electability, with longtime leader Marine Le Pen devoting extensive time and resources to its “de-demonization” campaign. This campaign has been a tremendous success in the party’s eyes, helping transform it from the fringe party that was crushed 82%-18% in the 2002 French presidential election to one viewed by many as the most likely winner of next year’s election. AfD is a different story. The party has thrived with its irreverence for Germany’s sterile political scene, paying little attention to established taboos. Though much of its rhetoric would not be out of place in the United States, the hypersensitivity of a country that distinguishes itself as having definitively left behind its nationalist past has little tolerance for narratives that depart from the consensus established during the reconstruction of the country after World War II. AfD’s leadership has largely gone to significant lengths to cull any language seen as sympathetic to the Nazi period of its history, but the party’s status as a decentralized coalition makes this more difficult than other, more message-disciplined parties on the continent. In May 2024, Maximilian Krah, an AfD member of the European Parliament, flew too close to the sun when, during an interview with the Italian daily Repubblica , he remarked that he “would never say that anyone who wore an SS uniform was automatically a criminal.” The comments led to a torrent of outrage from AfD’s then-ally, RN. AfD was expelled from their shared Identity and Democracy group, and two years later, relations still have not recovered between the right-wing front-runners of Europe’s two biggest countries. RN is not the only right-wing party that has clashed with AfD over matters of history — Poland’s right-wing parties are known to be especially sensitive toward the issue. The split has been institutionalized as well — RN and Fidesz co-founded the Patriots for Europe EP group, which, on July 8, 2024, became the third-largest in Europe with 84 members of the European Parliament. RN made up the largest constituency with 30 members, and other parties with representation include Fidesz, Italian Lega, the Czech ANO, Dutch PVV, Austrian FPO, Spanish Vox, Portuguese Chega, Belgian Vlaams Belang, and Danish DF. AfD is not represented. Part of the reason the split has remained in place is due to other issues the two parties clash on, mainly what to do with the EU and the Russia-Ukraine war. RN mainly follows leader Jordan Bardella’s stratagem of “change everything without destroying anything,” keeping the EU intact while changing its structure. AfD takes a firmer Euroskeptic stance. The Russia-Ukraine war is perhaps the most emotional break between the two. AfD is more neutral on the conflict and favors detente with Russia to diversify its international partnerships. RN is firmly on the side of Ukraine, sharing the strategy of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of adopting the consensus view on the war to better ingratiate itself with the European establishment. The schism has grown severe enough in recent months, with RN maneuvering in a way that almost seeks to box AfD out. The party has begun ingratiating itself with the center-right parties in Europe, primarily AfD’s rival Christian Democratic Union party, openly praising it while denigrating AfD. FORMER HUNGARIAN PRIME MINISTER VISITED WHITE HOUSE AND STATE DEPARTMENT In a May interview with a center-right German outlet, Bardella said many of AfD’s positions were “incompatible with our principles,” and liberally praised CDU Chancellor Friedrich Merz, an interview that shocked AfD lawmakers, especially due to Merz’s record-low approval ratings. AfD leader Alice Weidel suggested the remarks were made with ulterior motives. The urge to ingratiate itself with the establishment to cement its legitimacy stands as perhaps the biggest barrier to a true continent-wide, right-wing alliance as envisioned by figures such as Balazs Orban. For the time being, the impulse has driven a wedge between the two most powerful right-wing parties in Europe and could lower the other’s electoral chances. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy.text: By Sebastian Usher August was a brutal month for Ukraine. Russian aerial attacks increased significantly, launching thousands of drones. Kyiv was intensely bombarded, as were the southern cities of Mykolaiv and Odesa. Amid the destruction and loss of life, Odesa reported damage to six Unesco-protected sites, including the salmon-pink 19th Century Alexandru Sturdza House. It raised again the question of why it is so hard to hold actors accountable for the destruction of buildings and objects with real cultural significance. In the last month alone, Ukraine's Ministry of Culture reported that 148 cultural heritage sites were recorded as damaged or destroyed, including in Odesa. Several Ukrainian activist groups have tried to get accountability by lodging complaints with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Russia over cultural destruction and looting, but no indictments have been issued. Bijan Rouhani, a senior researcher at the Endangered Archaeology in the Middle East and North Africa project, says that the legal framework may be strong on paper but in practice it almost inevitably falls short. "No state actor has ever been tried for this offence. The obstacle is no longer evidence. We have satellite imagery, remote sensing and monitoring teams. The obstacle is jurisdiction and political will." Looking at the cauldron of conflicts convulsing the world, the question is ever more pressing as to whether effective action is possible to stop the damage being done or ensure accountability when it does. A casualty of war The conflict in Ukraine is just one of the panoply of wars in recent years that have revealed once again the disastrous impact of conflict on cultural heritage. Tareq Abu Dayyeh sells craftwork, souvenirs and antiquities in Gaza. The Great Omari Mosque features on many of the items he sells. It represents the very identity of Gaza - charting its history through the building's many manifestations from ancient pagan temple to Byzantine church to Seventh Century mosque to Crusader Cathedral and then back to being a mosque. The Great Omari Mosque was all but destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023. The Israeli military said the strike was targeting Hamas. Image source, LightRocket via Getty Images Image caption, The Great Omari Mosque in Gaza was largely destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023 Now Dayyeh says his heart is broken every time he sees the ruins. "When your past is destroyed, you have no present." The war in Gaza has claimed tens of thousands of lives and an estimated 200,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed by Israeli bombardment. But despite the overwhelming death and devastation, such cultural losses run deep. This is a sentiment expressed throughout history by people living through war. In Sudan, Lebanon, Yemen and Iran, the alarm has been raised time and time again. More than 100 sites in Iran are reported to have been damaged during the aerial war launched by the US and Israel back in February. They include the Unesco-listed Golestan Palace in the capital, Tehran, and Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan. The civil war in Sudan has further imperilled one of the ancient wonders of the world - the Meroe Pyramids, built during the flourishing civilisation of the Kingdom of Kush. Unesco, which designated Meroe as a World Heritage Site in 2011, has warned that the fighting has halted all preservation work there, leaving the fragile ancient structures prey to erosion from the encroaching sand and vegetation. A difficult task In response to the massive destruction of World War Two, the first-ever international treaty exclusively dedicated to protecting cultural heritage during armed conflict was adopted in The Hague in 1954. It applies to monuments and architecture, but also works of art and books, requiring states to safeguard and respect cultural property and refrain from any actions that might endanger it. Since the Hague Convention, there have been several additional moves to strengthen protective measures for cultural heritage. A Second Protocol to the Convention in 1999 said that any site that has been placed under enhanced protection due to its immense cultural significance must not be made a military target even if it is being used in such a way as to have become a 'military objective' - unless there is no other feasible way of ending its use in that way. When the International Criminal Court was established in The Hague in 2002, part of its remit was to bring accountability for deliberate attacks in war against buildings of religious, artistic and educational value as well as historical monuments, which had been defined as war crimes. But this has been a complex and difficult task. So far, only one case has been successfully brought at the ICC. Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi was a jihadist militant leader in Mali who was found guilty of directing attacks that destroyed mausoleums and a mosque in Timbuktu. He was sentenced to nine years in prison. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Ahmed al-Faqi al-Mahdi remains the only person successful prosecuted for this by the ICC Rouhani says that without the full backing of the major powers and a genuine commitment to international law and its enforcement, the world will simply keep watching the same devastating pattern repeat itself. "For most governments, heritage is a secondary concern, unless it becomes useful for propaganda," Rouhani says. "The Hague Convention requires states to build protection into their military rules and to respect cultural property abroad as well as at home. Looking at the scale of damage in recent conflicts, it is difficult to conclude that these obligations are taken seriously." In conflicts from Ukraine to Iran to Gaza, where schools and hospitals are seen as permissible military targets by combatants, how likely is it that a museum or pile of ancient stones, however freighted with beauty and history and memory, will be spared? Heritage ambulances In an isolated position in open countryside, a museum dedicated to the 18th Century Ukrainian philosopher and poet Hryhoriy Skovoroda was destroyed by Russian shelling during an overnight attack in 2022. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said it had left him speechless: "Targeted strikes against museums - not even terrorists would think of this. But this is the kind of army we are fighting against." The building was set ablaze and a caretaker was injured, but much of the collection had already been removed. Joe Biden, then the US president, said that Russian President Vladimir Putin was not only trying to take over Ukraine, but "literally trying to wipe out the culture and identity of the Ukrainian people". That pattern has been repeated across much of the frontline in Ukraine where local organisations have worked with international groups to try to safeguard their national heritage from Russian attack. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, A museum dedicated to the 18th Century Ukrainian philosopher and poet Hryhoriy Skovoroda was destroyed in a Russian attack One international group that's played a big role is the Aliph Foundation, which was set up in Geneva in 2017 to protect and repair cultural heritage. Alexandra Fiebig, a project manager with Aliph, says that her group provided millions of dollars in funds to Ukrainian museums scrambling to move their most valuable items to safety. This has involved the use of what she describes as 'heritage ambulances': "These vehicles that have specialised equipment and space with specialised teams and equipment, they were in the beginning travelling a lot to affected museums that were damaged through military action." Now, she says the teams also check on the artefacts that were transported in great haste to safer places to make sure they remain in good condition. Blue Shield International is a group that operates in multiple war zones, working with armed forces and local heritage officials to such an extent that it's come to be known as the Red Cross for culture. Dr Emma Cunliffe, the head of operations for the group, says Ukrainians are risking their lives to protect their heritage. "They are taking great measures to document the damage even when they are risking their own lives to do it. In fact one of the things we really see is that the government is taking huge steps despite the many many competing priorities and the struggles they are facing." Other conflicts have seen civilians take similar measures to protect their culture. In February 2015, Isis turned its attention from hacking down ancient statues and artefacts in Mosul in northern Iraq to ransacking its written heritage as its fighters laid waste to the city's much treasured public libraries. They burned the Central Library and destroyed or stole many thousands of books - many of them rare manuscripts that told the story of the city. Image source, The Asahi Shimbun via Getty Images Image caption, After seizing Mosul in 2014, Isis burned books in the city's Central Library "These were not simply books or shelves, they represented decades of knowledge and research and formed an important part of the intellectual heritage of Mosul University and the wider communityâ¦ Within days, everything was gone," Dr Mohammed Jasim Mohammed al-Hamdani says. The main library in Mosul has played a key role in his life - to such an extent that he is now the director there. "Seeing it destroyed felt like losing a part of myself. Many people in the city had a story connected to the University of Mosul and therefore the loss felt very close to home. And this is why when that part of Mosul was liberated from Isis, young people, old people rushed to the library to save what they could." A lucrative trade The obverse of communities taking it into their own hands to protect cultural property is the looting of those same sites. Again, this is a byproduct of war that dates back to the dawn of history. Cunliffe says that understanding the reasons for looting - which can vary from place to place - is a necessary starting point: "That might then in turn result in greater sanctions, greater prosecutions to take it seriously as a threat." She says that it's important if possible to convey a sense to local communities that by assisting this, they are selling their own heritage. In Iraq and Syria for example, both during and after the Isis rampage, looting of priceless artefacts was carried out on an industrial scale. The precious objects were spirited out and trafficked abroad, including to the US. A years-long investigation by the US Justice Department traced and tracked the smuggling routes and resulted in thousands of looted artefacts being returned to Iraq. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The looting of priceless artefacts in Iraq intensified during the Isis rampage In Europe and elsewhere, co-ordinated, multi-national police and customs operations take place regularly, seizing large numbers of stolen antiquities and arresting some of the traffickers. But the trade remains highly lucrative and the plethora of conflicts provides ever more opportunities. In Sudan, the national museum in Khartoum was stripped of its treasures in 2023 when it came under the control of one of the warring factions, the RSF, which loaded them onto trucks and left the display rooms bare. As in other conflict zones like Ukraine, specialised training has been provided for those involved in trying to recover the antiquities, which has had some success. But much of the museum's display - which told the story of the region over thousands of years - may have disappeared for good. Slim chance of deterrence The challenges of trying to limit the scale of destruction and looting of cultural heritage are huge. At an international or state level, there are regulations in place, but putting them into practice in a timely fashion is difficult enough - and often there isn't even the will to attempt this. Local initiatives backed by organisations like Aliph and Blue Shield International can make a difference on a small scale. But if - as seems the case right now - the chances of anyone facing consequences for destroying a heritage site are close to zero, then there is all but no real deterrent. Image source, Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images Image caption, Khaled al-Asaad was killed for refusing to give up Palmyra's secrets "What would change the calculation is not harsher sentences," says Dr Bijan Rouhani, "but a real prospect of being named - arrest warrants for the commanders who authorise these strikes, prosecutions in national courts under universal jurisdiction, and targeted sanctions on named individuals. Those measures don't require a new treaty. They require states to be willing to use the instruments they already have, against allies as well as adversaries." Of all the recent attempts to erase the cultural past embodied in stone, Palmyra in Syria still stands out. Isis blew up temples there and might have done far worse if it had not been defeated. One man became emblematic for standing up to them. For 40 years, the archaeologist Khaled al-Asaad had been the principal custodian of Palmyra. He was in his eighties when Isis descended on the ancient city. They captured him and tortured him to try to find out where its most valuable artefacts had been hidden. When he refused to tell them, they beheaded him in a public square and hung his corpse from a traffic light. Al-Asaad was celebrated across the world as a heroic defender of culture against the forces of darkness. He was awarded the Order of Civil Merit in Syria and in Palmyra, a school was named in his honour. But nothing is free from political complications. Years later, under the new authorities in Syria, his name has now been removed from the school.
